segments.english: These are the descendants of Noah's sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth: children were born to them after the flood.
segments.literal: and-these generations-of sons-of Noah Shem Ham and-Japheth and-were-born to-them sons after the-flood

tokens.note: wayyiqtol Niphal of ילד, passive: 'were born'

phrases.english: Noah's sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth
phrases.literal: 'sons-of Noah: Shem, Ham and-Japheth'; the three names stand in apposition
'and-were-born to-them sons'; ו rendered by a colon-like pause

grammar: תּוֹלְדֹת is a construct plural: the account of a man's descendants.
The etnaḥta on וָיָפֶת divides the verse: the list of names, then the new clause.
וַיִּוָּלְדוּ is a Niphal wayyiqtol, passive 'were born'.
segments.note: The English joins the two clauses with a colon, since the second states what follows from the first.

commentary.summary: Ramban's comment here is cut off in the pack and does not bear on the plain sense.

Ramban: men of those generations begot at about sixty, yet Noah's sons had no children even by a hundred, only after the flood; God restrained their fertility so that they would not beget children who would perish in the flood, or so that He would not have to save many in the ark. He did the same with the whole line (Lamech and Noah were late fathers), as Rashi cites from Bereshit Rabbah.
Radak says the verse tells us that Noah's sons did not have children in the ark.
Onkelos renders the verse closely: 'children were born to them after the flood'.

segments.english: The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.
segments.literal: sons-of Japheth Gomer and-Magog and-Madai and-Javan and-Tubal and-Meshech and-Tiras

phrases.english: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras
phrases.literal: seven names, each after the first joined by ו

grammar: The verse is a list; the final ו is rendered by 'and' before the last name only.
The zaqef qaton on יֶפֶת and on וּמָגוֹג, and the etnaḥta on וְתֻבָל, pace the list.
segments.note: Names are given in their familiar English forms.

commentary.summary: Rashi, citing Bereshit Rabbah: 'זוֹ פָּרַס' (this is Persia). The English keeps the name Tiras and does not identify it.
Ramban explains why Japheth is listed first, as the eldest, and Ham before Shem.
Radak cites Saadya's identification of Gomer with a later people; it does not bear on the English.

segments.english: The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.
grammar: The ו on וּבְנֵי links this list to the preceding one and is left unrendered.
The etnaḥta falls on גֹּמֶר, setting the father's name apart from the sons.
segments.note: MAM, the base text, reads אַשְׁכְּנַז with shva under the כ; WLC reads אַשְׁכֲּנַז with ḥataf pataḥ, and the pack's morpheme column follows WLC. The sense is the same.
apparatus: 10:3.3 אַשְׁכְּנַז: MAM shva under כ; WLC אַשְׁכֲּנַז, ḥataf pataḥ. No difference in sense.

segments.english: The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.
segments.literal: and-sons-of Javan Elishah and-Tarshish Kittim and-Dodanim

tokens.note: the pack's lexicon has רוֹדָנִים (Rhodians), the variant spelling with ר; the printed text has ד

grammar: Kittim has no ו before it: the etnaḥta on וְתַרְשִׁישׁ divides the four names into two pairs, Elishah and Tarshish, then Kittim and Dodanim, each pair joined by ו inside it.
Kittim and Dodanim are plural in form (-ים): names of peoples rather than of single men.
segments.note: The lexicon links the last name to רוֹדָנִים (Rhodians), reflecting the parallel reading in Chronicles. The data is kept; the English follows the Hebrew of this verse.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: Kittim is a name, and he is a son of Javan; he adds that the kingdoms of Greece and Rome are one. The English takes Kittim as a son's name.

apparatus: Chronicles (1 Chr 1:7) reads רוֹדָנִים for דֹּדָנִים; the lexicon in the pack records that form.

segments.english: From these the coastlands of the nations were separated in their lands, each according to its language, by their clans, in their nations.
segments.literal: from-these were-divided coasts-of the-nations in-their-lands man to-his-language to-their-clans in-their-nations

tokens.note: perfect Niphal 3rd plural, passive or reflexive: 'were separated'

phrases.english: From these the coastlands of the nations were separated
phrases.literal: 'from-these were-divided coasts-of the-nations'; the English puts the subject before the verb

phrases.english: by their clans, in their nations

grammar: מֵאֵלֶּה, 'from these', points back to the sons of Japheth just listed; the clause closes the list of Japheth's line.
נִפְרְדוּ is a Niphal perfect, 3rd plural, of פרד: 'were separated, spread apart'. Hebrew puts the verb before its subject אִיֵּי הַגּוֹיִם; the English puts the subject first.
אִיֵּי is the construct plural of אִי, 'coast, coastland, island'.
אִישׁ is distributive: 'each one'.
The four ב/ל phrases (lands, language, clans, nations) qualify the separation; the etnaḥta on לִלְשֹׁנוֹ divides them two and two.
segments.note: The English renders אִיֵּי הַגּוֹיִם literally, 'the coastlands of the nations' (lexicon: coast, region). The peoples who settled them are implied: Ramban takes the sons of Japheth as dwellers in the islands of the sea, each apart in his own land, and Radak takes אִיִּים as districts set apart from one another.

segments.english: The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan.
segments.literal: and-sons-of Ham Cush and-Egypt and-Put and-Canaan

phrases.literal: four names; מִצְרַיִם is the Hebrew name of Egypt and dual in form

grammar: מִצְרַיִם has a dual ending and is used as the name of the country and its people.
The etnaḥta on חָם separates the father's name from the sons.

segments.english: The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.
segments.literal: and-sons-of Cush Seba and-Havilah and-Sabtah and-Raamah and-Sabteca and-sons-of Raamah Sheba and-Dedan

phrases.english: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca

phrases.literal: 'and-sons-of Raamah'; the ו is left out in English because the sentence stops

grammar: The verse has two lists: the sons of Cush and, in a second clause, the sons of Raamah, one of them.
The etnaḥta on וְסַבְתְּכָא ends the first list.
segments.note: The lexicon spells שְׁבָא as Shᵉbâ; the English uses the familiar Sheba.

segments.english: Cush fathered Nimrod. He began to be a mighty man on the earth.
segments.literal: and-Cush begot [object-marker] Nimrod he began to-be mighty in-the-earth

tokens.note: Hiphil perfect 3ms of the geminate root חלל: הֵחֵל 'he began'. BDB files 'begin' (Hiph 2) in the same entry as 'profane'.

phrases.literal: object marker has no English counterpart

phrases.english: to be a mighty man on the earth

grammar: הוּא הֵחֵל is a fronted subject pronoun, giving emphasis: 'he, he began'.
גִּבֹּר is an adjective used as a noun: 'a mighty man'.
The etnaḥta on נִמְרֹד divides the statement of birth from the description.
segments.note: The English keeps 'began' for הֵחֵל and leaves open in what his might lay. Ibn Ezra: he began to show human might over the beasts, being a mighty hunter (10:9). Rashi: his might was to make the whole world rebel against God by the counsel of the generation of the Dispersion; this is recorded. Radak warns that the verse does not say no one was mighty before him, since the Nephilim were.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'לְהַמְרִיד כָּל הָעוֹלָם עַל הַקָּבָּ"ה בַּעֲצַת דוֹר הַפַּלָּגָה', to make the whole world rebel against God, by the counsel of the generation of the Dispersion. The English does not adopt this reading of גִּבֹּר.
Ibn Ezra: do not seek a meaning for every name; this does not bear on the English.
Ibn Ezra: 'he began to show the mighty deeds of men over the animals, for he was a mighty hunter'. The English follows this.
